title: Punctuation quick guide
intro: Punctuation tells your reader where a sentence begins, where it ends and how its parts fit together. Most marks have one main job, and once you know that job the choice is usually easy. The comma has the most jobs of all, so it has a table to itself, including the rule that stops the commonest mistake in student writing: two full sentences joined by a comma alone. The examples use British conventions.

tables.caption: Ending a sentence, and starting one
rows: Full stop  .
Ends a statement. One complete idea with a subject and a verb sits between two full stops.
The market opens at five in the morning.
Question mark  ?
Ends a direct question, but not a reported one.
Where is the library? · She asked where the library was.
Exclamation mark  !
Ends a strong exclamation. Keep it out of academic writing.
What a downpour!
Capital letter  A
Starts every sentence, and every proper name.
Our flight to Huế leaves on Tuesday.

tables.caption: The comma: when to use one, and when not to
rows: Two complete sentences
Never join them with a comma alone — that is a comma splice. Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a comma **plus** *and, but, or, so, for, nor, yet*.
✗ Traffic is heavy, many people are late. · ✓ Traffic is heavy, **so** many people are late. · ✓ Traffic is heavy**.** Many people are late.
Items in a list
Separate three or more items with commas.
We packed rice, water, a torch and a raincoat.
An introductory word, phrase or clause
Put a comma after anything that comes before the main subject.
**After the storm passed,** the ferries started again.
A subordinate clause at the end
No comma when the *because*, *if* or *when* clause comes second.
The ferries started again **because the storm had passed**.
Extra information
Use a pair of commas around information the sentence could do without.
My teacher**,** who studied in Huế**,** marks very quickly.
Essential information
Use no commas when the clause tells the reader *which one*.
The teacher **who studied in Huế** marks very quickly.
A transition word
Follow *however, therefore, moreover, in addition* with a comma when it opens a clause.
**However,** the results were very different.
Subject and verb
Never put a single comma between a subject and its verb.
✗ The students in my class, work very hard. · ✓ The students in my class work very hard.

tables.caption: Semicolon, colon, dash and brackets
rows: Semicolon  ;
Joins two complete sentences that belong closely together, with no conjunction between them.
The bus was full; we walked the last kilometre.
Semicolon  ;
Also separates list items that already contain commas.
The trip covered Huế, in the centre; Đà Nẵng, on the coast; and Hội An.
Colon  :
Introduces a list, an explanation or a quotation, and what comes before it must be a complete sentence.
We needed three things: a map, a torch and patience.
Dash  —
Marks a sharp break or an aside. Useful in an email, best avoided in an academic essay.
The result — and nobody expected this — was a draw.
Brackets  ( )
Hold information the reader could skip; the sentence must still work without them.
The survey (carried out in April) covered 300 families.

tables.caption: Apostrophes, quotation marks and capital letters
rows: Apostrophe  '  (possession)
Add 's to a singular noun, and just an apostrophe after a plural that already ends in -s.
the student's essay (one student) · the students' essays (several)
Apostrophe  '  (irregular plural)
A plural that does not end in -s still takes 's.
the children's books · the women's team
Apostrophe  '  (contraction)
Stands for the missing letters. Contractions suit emails, not formal essays.
it's = it is · don't = do not · they're = they are
Apostrophe  '  (never for plurals)
A plain plural never takes an apostrophe, and *its* meaning "belonging to it" has none either.
✗ two photo's · ✓ two photos · ✗ The city lost it's charm. · ✓ its charm
Quotation marks  ' '
Enclose the exact words of a source. British writing normally uses single marks.
The report calls the scheme 'a partial success'.
Quotation marks with other punctuation
Put a full stop or comma inside the marks only when it belonged to the original words.
She said, 'We will decide in May.' · He described it as 'slow', which surprised us.
Capital letters
Proper nouns, days, months, festivals, languages and nationalities all take one; seasons and school subjects do not.
On Monday in April we spoke Vietnamese and English. · We study maths every summer.
Capital letter  I
The pronoun *I* is always a capital, wherever it sits in the sentence.
My sister and I arrived late.

notes: The comma splice is the single most common punctuation error in student essays, because a comma is enough to join clauses in Vietnamese. Read your draft and check every comma: if a full sentence sits on each side of it, you need a conjunction, a semicolon or a full stop.
*However* is not a conjunction. *The bus was late, however we still arrived on time* is a comma splice; write *The bus was late; however, we still arrived on time* or start a new sentence.

A colon needs a complete sentence in front of it. *The team consists of: Mai, Long and Hải* is wrong; write *The team consists of Mai, Long and Hải* or *The team has three members: Mai, Long and Hải*.
British writing usually leaves out the comma before the final *and* in a list (*rice, water and a torch*). Add it only when leaving it out would confuse the reader.
Titles such as *Mr*, *Mrs*, *Ms* and *Dr* take no full stop in British writing, because the last letter of the short form is the last letter of the full word.
